name: V-Sit
description: The V-sit is an advanced isometric calisthenics hold in which the athlete balances on the tailbone with both arms and legs raised, forming a V-shape with the torso and legs. It simultaneously demands strong hip flexor strength and rectus abdominis tension to hold the torso upright against the hip-flexion load. The exercise requires significant core compression and spinal control, making it a progression from the hollow hold.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the floor with legs extended and hands lightly on the floor beside the hips.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a mat for comfort. No other equipment is required.
steps: Step 1: Sit tall with legs straight in front of you and hands beside your hips.
Step 2: Lean back slightly while simultaneously lifting both legs off the floor to approximately 45 degrees.
Step 3: Raise your arms forward parallel to the floor so they are pointing toward your feet.
Step 4: Balance on your tailbone and hold the V-shape, keeping the spine as long as possible.
Step 5: Hold for the prescribed duration, then lower with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe shallowly during the hold. Exhale as you raise into position and inhale to lower.
common_mistakes: Allowing the spine to collapse into a rounded C-shape instead of maintaining length
Bending the knees to make the hold easier when progression should come from time, not technique shortcuts
Letting the legs drop below 45 degrees due to insufficient hip flexor strength
safety_considerations: If hip flexor cramping occurs, lower legs immediately and stretch the hip flexors.
Avoid if experiencing lower back pain that is aggravated by sustained hip flexion.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Legs should form a 45-degree angle with the floor. The torso should lean back enough to counterbalance the legs.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold for 10–30 seconds. Build duration progressively.
coaching_cues: Sit tall through the crown of your head
Squeeze your thighs together and point your toes
Create a V — not a C
